turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've got a sunny balcony and I want to grow something I can actually eat.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lovely. Herbs, cherry tomatoes and salad greens all do well in pots. Which of those would you use the most?

contexts.pending: herbs, cherry tomatoes or salad greens
think_reask: So, which would you use most, herbs, tomatoes or salad greens?
Okay, time's up. What do you want on your balcony first?
Have you picked yet, herbs, cherry tomatoes or greens?
welcome_back: Welcome back! We were planning your balcony garden. Herbs, tomatoes or greens?
Hi again. You were choosing what to grow on your sunny balcony.
There you are. Any thoughts on what to plant first?

endings.user: Herbs, for sure. I'm always buying basil.
endings.moshi: Then start with basil, parsley and mint. Keep the mint in its own pot, it spreads like crazy.

endings.user: Cherry tomatoes. My kids would love picking them.
endings.moshi: Great choice. Get a big pot, a stake for support, and water them every day when it's hot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a bare patch in my back garden, maybe two meters wide, and it gets shade most of the day.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Shade is tricky but doable. Do you want flowers there, or something low-maintenance like ferns and ground cover?

contexts.pending: flowers or low-maintenance ferns for shady patch
think_reask: So, for that shady patch, flowers or something low-maintenance?
Alright, have you decided what kind of look you want for the shady spot?
welcome_back: Welcome back. We were talking about your shady patch. Flowers or ferns?
Good to have you back. Did you decide what to put in that bare spot?

endings.user: Some flowers would be nice, a bit of color.
endings.moshi: Try hostas, foxgloves and impatiens. They're happy in shade and still bring some color.

endings.user: Low-maintenance. I really don't have time.
endings.moshi: Then ferns and some ivy or periwinkle as ground cover. Once settled, they mostly look after themselves.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We're building raised beds this weekend. Wood or metal?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Wood looks natural and is cheaper, metal lasts longer and warms up faster in spring. What matters more to you, budget or durability?

think_reask: So, budget or durability? Wood or metal beds?
Okay, back to the raised beds. Have you decided on wood or metal?
welcome_back: Welcome back! We were picking material for your raised beds.
Hey, you're back. Still weighing up wood against metal?

endings.user: Budget, so let's go with wood.
endings.moshi: Good. Use untreated larch or cedar if you can, they resist rot without any chemicals.

endings.user: Metal. I don't want to rebuild them in five years.
endings.moshi: Sensible. Line the bottom with cardboard before you fill them, it smothers the weeds.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So the council finally gave me an allotment plot. It's waist high in brambles.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Congratulations, that's the hard part done. Do you want to clear the whole thing in one go, or cover half with sheeting and grow on the other half this year?

contexts.pending: clear the whole allotment or cover half and grow on the rest
think_reask: Right, the brambles. All at once, or half under sheeting for now?
So how are we tackling that plot, one big clearance or half and half?
welcome_back: The bramble jungle. One big push, or cover half and plant the rest?
We'd got to the allotment brambles. Leaning towards clearing it all, or doing half this year?

endings.user: Half and half. I'd like at least some potatoes this summer.
endings.moshi: Sensible. Black sheeting over the far half will weaken the roots while you get growing on the cleared side.

endings.user: All of it. I've got three weeks off and a lot of energy.
endings.moshi: Then dig the roots out rather than just cutting the tops, or they'll be back by June.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My gran gave me an orchid for my birthday and the leaves have gone all wrinkly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Wrinkly leaves usually mean thirsty roots. Can you see the roots through the pot? Are they silvery grey or green?

contexts.pending: whether the orchid roots look grey or green
think_reask: Okay, have a peek at those roots. Grey or green?
So what colour are the roots, silvery or green?
welcome_back: The orchid. Did the roots look grey or green?
Back to your gran's orchid. Any luck spotting what colour the roots are?

endings.user: Grey, and kind of papery.
endings.moshi: Then it's thirsty. Soak the whole pot in a bowl of room temperature water for ten minutes, then let it drain.

endings.user: Some are green but a few are brown and mushy.
endings.moshi: That's rot from too much water. Snip the mushy ones off with clean scissors and repot it in fresh bark.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I sit in a windowless office all day and I want one plant on my desk that won't die.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good news, a couple of plants actually cope with office lights. Would you like something that trails over the edge, or something tall and upright?

think_reask: So, for your desk, trailing or upright?
Time's up. Something that hangs down or something that stands tall?
welcome_back: Your desk plant. Trailing or upright, any preference yet?
So for that windowless office, are we going for something that spills over or something that stands up straight?

endings.user: Trailing. I like the idea of it creeping along the monitor.
endings.moshi: Then a pothos is your plant. Water it when the soil is dry and it'll forgive almost anything.

endings.user: Upright, I don't have much space.
endings.moshi: Go for a snake plant. It barely needs water, maybe once every three weeks under office lights.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My two boys want a sunflower contest this summer. Who grows the best one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: What a fun idea. Best meaning tallest, or best meaning the most flowers? That changes which seeds to buy.

contexts.pending: tallest or most flowers for the sunflower contest
think_reask: So what's the contest, tallest sunflower or most flowers?
Okay, which rule are you going with for the boys?
welcome_back: The sunflower contest. Are the boys competing on height, or on number of flowers?
So, have you settled the rules? Height or flower count?

endings.user: Tallest. They want to measure them against the shed.
endings.moshi: Then get a giant variety and give each one a strong cane. They'll need a sunny spot and lots of water in July.

endings.user: Most flowers, so nobody cries if one falls over.
endings.moshi: Smart parenting. Choose a branching variety, each plant can give you ten or more heads.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My neighbour's sycamore has grown so much it shades my whole veg patch now. I'm fuming.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's frustrating. You've got two routes, move the beds into the sunny side, or keep them and switch to crops that tolerate shade. Which feels less painful?

contexts.pending: move the veg beds or switch to shade tolerant crops
think_reask: So, shift the beds or change what you grow?
Right then, moving the patch or switching crops, which one?
welcome_back: The shaded veg patch. Moving the beds, or swapping to shade crops?
So about that sycamore situation. Relocate, or grow different things?

endings.user: I'll move them. I'm not giving up on tomatoes.
endings.moshi: Fair enough. Do it in autumn so the soil can settle over winter, and keep the compost from the old beds.

endings.user: Switch crops. I haven't got the back for moving soil.
endings.moshi: Then lettuce, chard, peas and herbs like parsley will still do well with a few hours of sun.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We need a hedge along the front for privacy, the road's got really busy.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Okay. Do you want it thick and tall quickly, even if it's a bit plain, or would you wait a few extra years for a mixed native hedge that birds love?

contexts.pending: fast plain hedge or slower mixed native hedge
think_reask: So which hedge, quick and plain, or slow and wild?
Have you decided how patient you want to be with this hedge?
welcome_back: The front hedge. Fast and plain, or slower and mixed?
Where did you land on the hedge, speed or wildlife?

endings.user: Fast. The traffic noise is driving us mad.
endings.moshi: Then a privet or laurel hedge will fill out in two or three years. Trim it twice a year to keep it dense.

endings.user: Mixed native. We're in no rush, honestly.
endings.moshi: Lovely. Hawthorn, hazel and holly together give you flowers, berries and some green in winter.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to plant garlic this autumn. Never done it before.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Easy and very satisfying. Do you want big cloves that store for months, or the kind with a flower stalk you can eat in early summer?

contexts.pending: long storing garlic or the kind with edible flower stalks
think_reask: So, storage garlic or the one with the stalks?
Okay, which garlic are we planting?
welcome_back: Your garlic. Long keeping cloves, or the stalky kind?
We'd got to the garlic choice. Have you picked a type?

endings.user: The one that keeps. I go through tons of it.
endings.moshi: Then go for a softneck variety. Plant the cloves pointy end up, about a hand's width apart.

endings.user: The stalks sound fun, let's do those.
endings.moshi: That's hardneck garlic. Snap the curly stalks off in June and fry them in butter, they're delicious.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My daughter's getting married next September and I'd love to grow some of the flowers myself.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a beautiful plan. Are you picturing big showy dahlias, or something soft and scented like sweet peas?

contexts.pending: dahlias or sweet peas for the wedding
think_reask: So, dahlias or sweet peas for the wedding?
Have you pictured it yet? Big dahlias or soft sweet peas?
welcome_back: The wedding flowers. Showy dahlias or scented sweet peas?
So, for your daughter's big day, which flowers are you growing?

endings.user: Dahlias. September is their best month, isn't it?
endings.moshi: It is, perfect timing. Order the tubers in spring and plant a few extra in case some sulk.

endings.user: Sweet peas, she loves the smell.
endings.moshi: Then sow them early and keep picking. Just know they can fade by September, so a late sowing in June helps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We're away for two weeks in August and I'm worried about all my pots.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Two weeks in August is a long time for pots. Would you rather set up a little drip watering kit, or ask a neighbour to pop round?

contexts.pending: drip watering kit or ask a neighbour
think_reask: So, gadget or neighbour for the pots?
Okay, for the holiday, drip kit or a friendly neighbour?
welcome_back: The pots while you're away. A drip kit, or a neighbour?
So for those two weeks, have you picked how the pots get watered?

endings.user: A kit. I don't want to owe anyone a favour.
endings.moshi: Fair. Test it for a few days before you leave, so you can adjust how much each pot gets.

endings.user: The neighbour. She offered last year, actually.
endings.moshi: Lovely. Group the pots together in the shade so it's quick for her, and leave a bottle of wine as thanks.

turns.speaker: user

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: No, I thought you did.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The can, the hose is too strong for the seedlings next to them.

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: Okay, on it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Look at these leaves. Do you think something's eating them?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Great. What do your parents use against slugs?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How often should I water my houseplants?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most like to dry out a bit between waterings. Push a finger into the soil, and if the top few centimeters are dry, it's time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So not on a fixed schedule?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not really. In winter they need much less, and in summer they might need it twice a week.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have a cactus and a / what's it called, a peace lily.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Those are opposites. Water the cactus maybe once a month, and the peace lily when its leaves start to droop a little.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, it droops? I thought that meant it was dying.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's just being dramatic. Give it a good drink and it usually perks up within a few hours.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: When should I plant tulip bulbs?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: In autumn, once the soil has cooled down. Late October to November is usually ideal.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How deep do they go?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: About three times the height of the bulb, so roughly fifteen to twenty centimeters, pointy end up.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And can I put them in pots? I was hoping to / put a few by the front door.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, tulips look great in pots. Pack them closely together and make sure the pot drains well.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do they come back every year?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some do, but many fade after the first year. Lots of people just plant fresh ones each autumn.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to start composting but I live in a flat. Is that even possible?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is. A small worm bin or a bokashi bucket can live under your sink and won't smell if you look after it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Worms in my kitchen? My partner would / probably move out.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then bokashi might be easier. It's a sealed bucket where you add scraps and a sprinkle of bran, no worms involved.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What do I do with it when it's full?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Bury it in soil, a large planter or a community garden bed. After a few weeks it turns into rich compost.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a community garden two streets over actually.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect, ask them. Most community gardens are happy to take it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My lawn has yellow patches all over. What's going on?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Common causes are dry weather, dog pee or grubs in the soil. Do you have a dog?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah, a big one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's likely it then. Watering the spot right after the dog goes can dilute it and stop the burn.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I can't follow him around with a watering can all day.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fair. You could train him to use one corner of the garden, or reseed the patches in spring.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Reseeding sounds easier. Do I just / throw seeds on top?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Rake the patch first to loosen the soil, then sprinkle the seed and keep it moist for two weeks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: When am I supposed to prune roses? My mother in law says February, the internet says everything.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Late winter is a good rule for most shrub roses, just as the buds start to swell. So February or early March, depending on where you live.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, she wins this round. How much do I cut off?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Roughly a third to a half. Take out anything dead or crossing first, then cut just above an outward facing bud.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Outward facing, meaning / pointing away from the middle of the bush?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. That keeps the centre open so air moves through, which helps stop black spot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And the climbing one on the fence? Same treatment?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Gentler. Tie the long canes in sideways and just shorten the little side shoots to a couple of buds.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My tomato seedlings are tall and spindly and falling over. Did I do something wrong?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's called legginess, and it's really common. They're stretching towards the light because they aren't getting enough.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They're on the kitchen windowsill though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Even a bright window is dim compared to outside in early spring. Turning the tray every day helps, and a cheap grow light helps a lot more.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I save these ones or should I / just start again?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Tomatoes are great at this, you can save them. When you pot them on, bury the stem right up to the first leaves. It'll grow roots all along it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Wait, really? Bury the stem?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Really. It's one of the few plants that loves it. You'll end up with sturdier plants than if they'd never flopped.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Black bugs all over my broad beans. Thousands of them.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sounds like blackfly. They love the soft tips of broad beans. Are they clustered right at the top?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yep. Like a little black hat.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then pinch the tops off, bugs and all. The beans are usually tall enough by then, and it stops the worst of it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't want to spray anything, we've got / a lot of ladybirds around actually.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good, leave them to it. Ladybird larvae eat aphids like crazy. A spray would kill them too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The tops I pinch, can I eat those?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can, once you've rinsed the bugs off. Steam them like spinach, they taste a bit like the beans.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to grow potatoes but I've only got a patio. Is that daft?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not daft at all. Potatoes grow well in big bags or tubs, and tipping them out at harvest is honestly the best bit.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How big are we talking?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Something around the size of a laundry basket, with drainage holes. Three seed potatoes per bag is plenty.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I fill it all the way up from the start?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No, start with a bit of compost, put the potatoes in, and cover them lightly. As the leaves grow, keep adding compost around them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why's that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The buried stem makes more potatoes, and it keeps them out of the light so they don't turn green.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, green potatoes are bad, right? My dad always / cut those bits off.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Your dad was right. The green parts can upset your stomach, so cut them away or skip them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Every autumn I throw out my geraniums and buy new ones in spring. Feels wasteful.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is a bit. You can keep them over winter quite easily if you've got a cool, frost free spot, like a porch or a spare room.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's an unheated porch. Gets cold but never freezes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's ideal. Dig them up before the first frost, cut them back by about half, and pot them up snugly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do they need watering all winter?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Hardly at all. Just a splash once a month so the roots don't completely dry out. They'll look sad, and that's fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And then in spring?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Bring them somewhere brighter, water more, and they'll push out new shoots. You can even take cuttings and double your plants for free.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How short should I cut the lawn? I just bought a new mower and I'm itching to use it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For most garden lawns, around four or five centimetres is a happy height. Going shorter tends to stress the grass.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My neighbour cuts his like a golf course.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It looks sharp, but very short grass dries out faster and lets moss and weeds in. His probably needs a lot more feeding and watering.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha, he is always out there with a sprinkler. How often should I mow?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: In spring and early summer, about once a week. The rule of thumb is never cut off more than a third of the height at once.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And in a heatwave?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Raise the blades and mow less. Taller grass shades its own roots and stays greener.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hey, quick one. The garden centre has peat free compost and normal compost. Does it matter which?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It matters for the environment. Peat comes from bogs that take thousands of years to form, so peat free is the kinder choice.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it worse for the plants though?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The good peat free brands are pretty much as good now. They can dry out on top while still being wet underneath, so check with your finger before watering.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. And for seeds? I'm doing / chillies and some flowers.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Get a fine peat free seed compost for those. It's lighter and has fewer nutrients, which seedlings actually prefer.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Right, seed compost for seeds, the big bag for everything else.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's it. Simple as that.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So my nephew put an avocado stone in water with toothpicks and now it's got a root. What now?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a great start. Once the root is a few centimetres long and a shoot appears at the top, it's ready for a pot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Will it ever make avocados?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Honestly, probably not indoors. Trees from stones can take ten years or more and often need warmth we can't give them. But it makes a lovely leafy houseplant.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He's going to be gutted. He wanted guacamole.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe sell it to him as a tree he grew himself. Kids usually love watching it shoot up, it can grow really fast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fair point. What pot / should we use, something big?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Medium to start, with good drainage. Leave the top half of the stone above the soil, and keep it in a bright spot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why are my cucumbers bitter? I was so proud of them.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Bitterness usually comes from stress, mostly uneven watering or big swings in temperature.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I did go away for a long weekend. They were bone dry when I got back.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That'll do it. Cucumbers want steady moisture. A deep drink every day or two in hot weather keeps them sweet.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I fix the ones that are already growing?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some bitterness is near the stalk end and in the skin. Peel them and cut off the top bit, and they're often fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, phew. Any variety that's / less fussy for next year?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look for ones described as burpless or bitter free. They've been bred to be much less likely to turn bitter.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My lawn is more moss than grass at this point. Is it even worth fighting?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It depends. Moss loves shade, damp and compacted soil. If your lawn has all three, it'll keep coming back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Shady, yes. Damp, yes. Compacted, probably, the kids play football on it constantly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you could rake the moss out in autumn, spike the soil with a fork for drainage, and overseed with a shade tolerant grass mix.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds like a lot.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is a solid afternoon. The other option is accepting the moss. It's soft, green and stays that way without mowing much.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Honestly, a moss lawn / sounds kind of nice.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Plenty of people go that way. It won't love the football though, so maybe keep one patch of tough grass for the goal.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want my garden to be good for bees. Where do I even start?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start with flowers that are easy for them to get into. Open, simple flowers are better than big fluffy double ones.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like what?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lavender, foxgloves, catmint, comfrey, and herbs left to flower, like thyme and oregano.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I didn't know herbs count.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They're some of the best. Also aim for something in flower from early spring to late autumn, so there's always food around.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's good early? Spring is / kind of bare in my garden.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Crocuses and pussy willow are lifesavers for early bees. Plant some crocus bulbs in the lawn this autumn.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And I should stop spraying the dandelions, I guess.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes please. Dandelions are a proper bee buffet in April.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Monstera roots are coming out the bottom of the pot. Time to repot?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sounds like it. Spring or early summer is the best time, when it's growing actively.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's huge though. How do I even get it out?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Water it the day before, then lay the pot on its side and ease it out. Get someone to hold the stems so nothing snaps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How much bigger should the new pot be?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Only a size or two up. A pot that's way too big holds extra water and the roots can rot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's also got these long brown / ropey things coming out of the stem.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Those are aerial roots. They're normal. You can tuck them into the soil or give it a moss pole to climb.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My rhubarb has these tall stalks with big frilly flower things on top. Is that okay?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's it trying to flower, which pulls energy away from the stalks. Cut the flower stems off at the base as soon as you see them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I still eat the normal stalks?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, they're fine. Pull them rather than cutting, give a little twist near the base.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: When should I stop picking? I've been / taking loads.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Stop around early summer. The plant needs its leaves after that to build up strength for next year.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And the leaves, those are poisonous right?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, don't eat the leaves. They're fine on the compost heap though.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The forecast says frost tonight and my dahlias are still out. Help.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Don't panic. One light frost will blacken the leaves, but the tubers underground are usually fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So should I dig them up now?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Wait until after the frost blackens the foliage, then cut the stems down and lift the tubers within a few days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Then what? Do I just / shove them in the garage?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Let them dry upside down for a day or two, then store them in a box of dry compost or newspaper somewhere cool but frost free.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And my lemon tree in the pot?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That one needs to come in tonight. Lemons hate frost. A cool bright room or porch is perfect.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My strawberry plants are sending out long stringy runners everywhere.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Those runners are baby plants on a leash. You can either snip them off or use them to make new plants for free.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Free plants, go on.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pin the little plantlet onto a pot of compost with a bent wire or a stone. Once it's rooted in a few weeks, cut the runner.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is there a catch?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you leave too many on, the mother plant puts energy into them instead of fruit. Keep two or three per plant, cut the rest.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And how long do / the old plants last?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: About three or four years before they tire out. That's why rooting runners every summer keeps the bed going.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it true you can change hydrangea colours? My blue one went pink after I moved it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's true for many mophead and lacecap hydrangeas. The colour depends on the soil. Acidic soil gives blue, alkaline gives pink.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So my new spot is alkaline.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very likely. If you want blue back, you can grow it in a pot of ericaceous compost, or add a blueing product to the soil.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is that like chemicals?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's aluminium sulphate usually, and it works slowly. Honestly, a pot of acidic compost is the easier route.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I kind of like the pink though. My wife / says it looks like candy floss.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then leave it. It's happy, it's pink, and you get to skip the chemistry homework.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Morning or evening, when's the best time to water the garden?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Early morning is usually best. The plants get a drink before the heat and the leaves dry off quickly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm not a morning person.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Evening is fine too, just water the soil rather than the leaves. Wet leaves overnight can invite mildew and slugs.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Slugs! Those things have eaten / half my lettuces this year.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then morning watering really would help. Slugs love a damp evening.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ugh, fine. How long should I water for?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Less often but deeper is better. A good soak twice a week beats a light sprinkle every day.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. Setting an alarm, apparently.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Even ten minutes with a hose before work is enough for most beds.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want a gardening thing to do with my four year old. Something quick, she's not patient.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Cress is the classic for a reason. Sprinkle seeds on damp cotton wool and you'll see shoots in two or three days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Two days, that's perfect. Can we make it fun?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Grow it in an empty eggshell with a face drawn on. The cress becomes hair, and she can give it a haircut with scissors.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh she'll love that. Then what?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then sunflowers or radishes. Radishes go from seed to plate in about a month, and they're bright red.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Will she actually eat a radish? She's / very suspicious of anything red.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe not, but kids are much more likely to try food they grew themselves. Worth a go.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm putting a water butt by the shed. Is it worth it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very. Plants actually prefer rainwater, and you'll save on your bill in summer.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I connect it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You fit a diverter kit into the shed's downpipe. It sends rain into the butt and back down the pipe once the butt is full.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The shed doesn't have a gutter.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ah, then you'll need to add one. A short length of plastic gutter and a downpipe is cheap and pretty easy to screw on.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Right. Anything else I / should know before buying?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Get one with a lid so it doesn't breed mosquitoes, and raise it on a stand so a watering can fits under the tap.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I planted mint in the border last year. It's now in the lawn, the path and I think the neighbour's garden.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Classic mint. It spreads by underground runners and it's very good at it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So how do I kill it off?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Dig out as much as you can, especially those white runners. Expect to keep pulling bits for a season or two.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Brilliant. So I can never have mint again?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can, just in a pot. Even better, sink the pot into the ground with the rim above the soil. Looks planted, but it's caged.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And I owe / my neighbour an apology, don't I.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe an apology and a mojito. They've got plenty of mint now.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We want to grow a giant pumpkin for Halloween. Like, really giant.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Love it. Pick a giant variety and start the seeds indoors in late April or early May.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And then?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Plant it out after the last frost in a really rich spot, loads of manure or compost. They're very hungry plants.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We've got space next to the compost heap.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's actually a perfect spot. Once a few pumpkins form, keep only the best one, so the plant feeds just that.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Only one? That / feels a bit harsh.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's harsh but that's the secret. Water it deeply and often, and slide a board under the pumpkin so it doesn't rot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How big could it get?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: In a good summer, big enough that you'll need two people to lift it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There are tiny black flies around my houseplants. They come out every time I water.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Those are probably fungus gnats. They breed in damp compost, and the larvae live in the top layer of soil.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Gross. Are they hurting the plants?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Mostly they're just annoying, though lots of larvae can nibble seedling roots.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I get rid of them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Let the top few centimetres dry out between waterings, that breaks their cycle. Yellow sticky traps catch the adults.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I do water a lot, to be fair. I / kind of love my watering can.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a common one. Try watering from below, standing the pots in a tray for twenty minutes. The surface stays dry and the gnats give up.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Our new house has a steep sloping garden. Mowing it is honestly dangerous.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Slopes are tough. Many people terrace them, or swap the grass for plants that hold the soil and never need mowing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Terracing sounds expensive.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can be if you hire a team. A cheaper route is ground cover plants and shrubs, with a simple path of steps across it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What kind of ground cover?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For sun, creeping thyme, rock roses and low junipers. For shade, periwinkle and some hardy geraniums.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And to stop the soil / sliding down when it rains?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Mulch with bark chips and use a biodegradable jute matting while the plants get going. The roots will hold it after a year or two.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My lavender's gone all woody and bald at the bottom. Can I cut it hard?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Unfortunately lavender usually doesn't regrow from old bare wood. If you cut into it, those stems often stay bare.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Well that's depressing.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is. The good news is lavender is cheap and easy to replace, and you can take cuttings from the green tips first.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I stop the new ones going the same way?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Trim them every year right after flowering, taking off the flower stalks and a bit of the green. Never go into the brown.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've literally never / pruned it once in six years.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it did really well to last that long. Start fresh and give the new ones a trim every August.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I rent a basement flat. One small north facing window. Can I grow herbs at all?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some, yes. Mint, parsley and chives handle lower light better than sunny herbs like basil or rosemary.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Basil was the one I wanted, of course.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Of course. You could grow basil under a small clip on grow light. They're cheap now, and it makes a huge difference.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does it need to be on all day?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: About twelve to fourteen hours. A plug timer makes it effortless.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, so chives and parsley on the sill, basil under the light. Do I / buy seeds or plants?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For basil, honestly, a supermarket pot works. Split it into three or four clumps and repot them, they'll grow much better.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I save seeds from my tomatoes for next year?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can, as long as they're not hybrids. If the packet said hybrid, the new plants might not match the parent.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: These are old heirloom ones from my uncle.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect, those come true from seed. Pick a really ripe tomato and scoop the seeds into a jar with a little water.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And then?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Leave it a few days until it gets a bit mouldy on top. That ferments away the jelly coating. Then rinse and dry the seeds on a plate.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mouldy on purpose. That's / disgusting and brilliant.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's the traditional way. Store them dry in a paper envelope, labelled, somewhere cool. They'll keep for years.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a huge tree stump in the middle of my garden. Any way to get rid of it without a machine?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can, it just takes patience. Drill some deep holes in the top, fill them with water and cover it so it stays damp. That speeds up rotting.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long are we talking?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A year or two for a big stump. Fungi and bugs do most of the work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's ages.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is. The quicker route is hiring a stump grinder for a day. It turns the stump into wood chips in an hour or so.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Or I could / just make it a feature, I suppose?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a lovely option. Put a big pot on top, or let ferns and moss grow around it. Beetles will love it too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'd like to turn part of the lawn into a wildflower meadow. Can I just scatter seeds?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sadly, scattering seed on lawn rarely works. Grass is too competitive and smothers the seedlings.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So what's the trick?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Strip off the turf in that patch, and don't add compost. Wildflowers actually like poor soil. Then sow in autumn or spring.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Poor soil, okay, my garden is great at that.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you're halfway there. Another trick is a plant called yellow rattle. It weakens the grass so flowers can get in.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And do I mow it ever?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Once a year in late summer, after the flowers set seed. Leave the cuttings a few days so the seeds drop, then rake them up.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sounds good. I'll mark out / a patch by the back fence this weekend.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start small, maybe a couple of metres square. You can always expand it once you see what comes up.

option_sets.lead_in: I've got one empty bed in the backyard and I can't decide what to plant.
options: The first idea is tomatoes and peppers, which need a lot of sun and regular watering.
Then there's a herb garden with basil, mint and rosemary, small and easy to keep up.
And the last one is wildflowers for the bees, basically no work once they're in the ground.
moshi_comment: If that bed gets full sun, tomatoes and peppers would give you the most to eat, but they need daily attention in summer. The herbs are easy and you'll use them all the time in the kitchen. Wildflowers are the lowest effort and great for bees.

How much time do you want to spend out there each week? If you love being in the garden, go for the tomatoes. If not, herbs give you something useful without much work, just keep the mint in a pot or it'll take over.

option_sets.lead_in: Our lawn looks terrible and I'm trying to figure out what to do with it.
options: One option is to reseed the whole thing in the fall and water it a lot for a few weeks.
Another is to lay new sod, which looks perfect right away but costs a lot more.
Or we could replace part of it with a gravel patio and some low plants that don't need much water.
moshi_comment: Reseeding in the fall is the cheapest way to get a nice lawn, it just takes patience. Sod is instant, but you're paying a lot for that speed. The gravel patio is a nice idea if you're tired of mowing and watering.
Do you actually use the lawn, like for kids or a dog? If so, I'd reseed in the fall. If it's mostly for looks, the patio with low water plants could save you a lot of work in the long run.

option_sets.lead_in: I've got room for exactly one fruit tree and I keep changing my mind.
options: There's an apple on a dwarf rootstock, so it stays small and fruits in a couple of years.
Or a fig trained against the south wall, which would love the warmth there.
A plum is another one, but I've heard they crop like mad one year and then hardly at all.
And maybe a cherry, though the birds would probably get most of them.
moshi_comment: The dwarf apple is the steady, reliable pick, and you'll get fruit quickly. The fig on that warm wall is tempting if you love figs, it'll look great too. The plum and cherry are lovely but come with the boom and bust years and the bird battle.

Which fruit do you actually eat most? If it's apples, go dwarf apple and you'll never regret it. If you want something a bit special, the fig against the south wall is a treat that most neighbours won't have.

option_sets.lead_in: The gravel drive is full of weeds again and I want to pick a method that actually works.
options: One idea is just pouring boiling water from the kettle on them every week or so.
Another is buying a gas weed burner, which looks fun but a bit scary.
Or we rake all the gravel off, put down a proper membrane, and put the gravel back.
moshi_comment: Boiling water works on small weeds but you'll be doing it forever. The burner is quicker, though deep roots often come back. Redoing the membrane is a weekend of hard work, but it's the only one that stops most weeds for years.

How long are you staying in the house? If it's years, the membrane job is worth the sore back. If it's short term, the kettle or the burner will keep things tidy enough, just be careful with the burner near the hedge.

option_sets.lead_in: My new flat is on the tenth floor and the balcony is so windy. I need plants that cope.
options: I was looking at ornamental grasses, they sway around and apparently don't snap.
Lavender is another idea, because it's tough and smells nice when you brush past.
Or succulents in heavy pots, since they hold onto water and stay low.
moshi_comment: Grasses are made for wind, they bend instead of breaking and look lovely moving. Lavender is tough too and handles dry, breezy spots well. Succulents are fine as long as the pots are heavy, but some get scorched in that much wind and sun.
I'd mix the first two. Grasses for height and movement, lavender lower down for scent. Keep the succulents for the most sheltered corner, and use heavy pots for all of them so nothing takes off.

option_sets.lead_in: I want a winter project to help me start seeds earlier next year.
options: A small glass greenhouse would be the dream, but it costs a lot and needs a flat base.
A wooden cold frame is cheap, and I could probably build it myself from old windows.
Or a polytunnel, which gives tons of space but I'm worried it looks ugly.
moshi_comment: The cold frame is the easy win, cheap, quick and fine for hardening off seedlings. A greenhouse is lovely and lasts, but it's a bigger project with that base. The polytunnel gives you the most growing room for the money, if you can live with the look.
If this is your first year starting seeds early, I'd build the cold frame from those old windows. It'll teach you a lot. If you catch the bug, you can save up for the greenhouse later.
